**My reasoning:**

I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and corn here, and so did his father. The soil is flat and the land is good for it. I have about 8 mu contracted from the village. There's no reason to try something new at my age — I know what this land does, I know the buyers at the local grain station, and my neighbors all do the same rotation.

After the wheat comes off in June, I put corn in right away on the same ground. Same 8 mu. That's how it always works here. You don't leave the land idle.

For wheat seed, I buy whatever the seed shop in town has — it's always some improved variety now, been that way for twenty years. For corn I use hybrid, same as everyone. I wouldn't grow traditional corn, nobody does anymore.

I water the wheat four times: once before sowing to get a good seedbed, once before winter sets in, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. Corn gets one irrigation at the silking stage if July is dry — usually the summer rains handle the rest.

I put down compound fertilizer as the base and then urea on top during the season. I know I use a lot of fertilizer but the yield suffers if I cut back, and I can't afford that. My back isn't what it was so for the corn I just let the seed drill go in after the wheat stubble — no tilling. For wheat I still rotary-till in autumn.

For pesticides, wheat gets a herbicide spray in spring and I watch for rust — if it comes I spray once more. Corn I spray herbicide right after planting, that's usually enough.

Wheat needs four irrigations given Quzhou's dry springs, while maize mostly relies on summer rain with one supplemental watering at silking if needed. I rotary-till before wheat sowing but go no-till for maize to save my back and cut labor.
